As we know, NixOS is currently very intertwined with systemd. However, many people do not like or want to use systemd for different reasons.

How feasible would it be to untangle NixOS from systemd, to finally have the ability to choose a different init system on NixOS?

For example, one could set a `boot.initSystem` option in their NixOS config to choose their init system as such:

```nix
boot.initSystem.package = pkgs.systemd
boot.initSystem.package = pkgs.openrc
boot.initSystem.package = pkgs.runit
# ...
```

While this would probably break modular services, an idea I had was  to have a high-level service configuration format in Nix that would eventually generate a service file for each init system.

posts.name: Arnout Engelen
posts.raw: If you’re interested in this, I think your best bet would be to look into the currently-in-development ‘modular services’ ( https://nixos.org/manual/nixos/stable/#modular-services ). I haven’t used them, but AFAICT in theory that would allow you to move ‘most’(?) of the logic from the NixOS module to the nixpkgs modular service, and then build an alternative to NixOS that doesn’t use the NixOS modules but uses these modular services instead.

This looks promising, although I wonder if user services should be delegated to home-manager. 

If all of the `services.<insert thing here>` could be migrated over to modular services, I feel like this whole init-freedom thing could become a lot more feasible.

An issue I do see, however, (not related to modular services) is having to port the Stage 1 boot over to all of the init systems. Since NixOS no longer uses the shell script-based stage 1, we'd have to move stage 1 over to *every* init system supported, or force `boot.initrd.systemd.enable = false` for users whose initsystem != systemd, and fall back to the old stage 1

nixpkgs and the nixos module system is modular enough that such an effort can be pioneered outside of nixpkgs.

There's already sisox https://codeberg.org/amjoseph/sixos

Honestly I don't really like the complexity supporting multiple init systems bring to NixOS. I'm not a fan of [modular services](https://nixos.org/manual/nixos/stable/#modular-services) either.

posts.name: Will Fancher
posts.raw:
[quote="lav, post:18, topic:78333"]
the way all their services work are fairly similar
[/quote]

That's really not true. There's a lot of different aspects of service management that differ quite a bit between service managers. For instance, systemd's concept of "units" is really unique because dependencies come in the form of both event propagation rules (`Wants=`, `PartOf=`, `Triggers=`, etc.) as well as job ordering queues (`After=`, `Before=`). The semantics of these things are very often critical to how the unit functions. For instance imagine a service that depends on a certain file system and should not listen on the network until the firewall starts. In systemd, you can just order a socket unit after the firewall unit, and you can have the socket unit trigger a service unit that depends on a mount unit. The socket isn't listening until after the firewall is up, and a user connecting triggers an on-demand startup of the service, which queues jobs to mount the corresponding file system first after waiting for its block device to appear.

How would you do that with another service manager? I'm not saying you couldn't; I'm just saying that with systemd every single behavior I just touched on *is a property of a unit*, whereas in other systems all of those things would be done *completely differently*. I'm sure that implementing this example is perfectly reasonable in your service manager of choice, but to say that the implementation would be fairly similar to how you do it with systemd is certainly not true. You would not be making things analogous to systemd units with properties analogous to systemd unit properties. macOS's launchd, for instance, basically only has the socket-activated part of that equation. Others are more similar and others still are more different. The point is that there's a wide variety of ways different systems do these things.

And that's just dependency management. There's all sorts of other massive differences. Bootup, UID allocation, sandboxing, runtime administration (e.g. the things `switch-to-configuration` does), device / driver management, and logging are all completely different depending on the service manager. There's all kinds of differences that majorly influence how you implement your use case on that service manager.

I have become very convinced that you cannot make an abstraction layer for portability between service managers without that layer being so large and complicated as to constitute a service manager itself; it would just be a custom service manager implemented in terms of other service managers.

[quote="ksvivek, post:53, topic:78333"]
No one would have thought that there’s a Linux OS where they can just change few lines and apply to get a whole mew DE without any other manual work.
[/quote]

Don't be fooled by this analogy. Yes, the DE is a fairly large part of the operating system that impacts how it's used pretty heavily. But the way that other software interacts with it is pretty much standardized. The reason you can swap out one DE with another is because applications have all agreed upon standards like X11 / wayland / pulseaudio / pipewire / a zillion others. The hole the DE fills is very standards-shaped.

The same can't be said for service managers. They are simply not striving to implement the same interfaces, and designing standard interfaces and implementing the adapters between them and the service managers is difficult. NixOS doesn't really have this problem with DEs. DEs are already implementing ubiquitous standards. It's comparatively easy to swap out DEs because we don't have to do the work to adapt applications to different DEs. As I've said before in this thread, creating an abstraction like that is tantamount to creating an entire custom service manager, except you also need to implement a backend for every service manager you want to support. And again, I don't mean to say this isn't possible. But that is a monumental task; far far bigger than what's involved in swapping the DE, because the DE and the applications already did the work of making them swappable.

Furthermore, since standards like that don't exist for service management, we generally just get systemd unit files from upstream applications. And that's extremely useful; being able to use the upstream's service definition (i.e. `systemd.packages = [ foo ];`, which uses the unit files shipped in the `foo` package) rather than having to define everything ourselves in nixpkgs is huge. So for this service management abstraction to work, you don't just need it to *exist* (which is already hard enough), you also need upstreams to buy into it and ship service packages for it. At the very least that means the abstraction needs to be something with broad appeal outside of NixOS, but it also means gathering a lot of consensus across the Linux universe.

That's sort of what wayland was up against, because it also needed to get a lot of buy-in from all across the ecosystem. But wayland has taken forever for everyone to actually converge on, and it now represents a bunch of standard protocols that a bunch of parties all agreed on, which is just really hard. And this is kind of a best case for these kinds of efforts; wayland only had to get buy-in from a relatively small number of libraries to cover a large percentage of use cases, it's relatively straightforward for xwayland to exist for everything else, and the various wayland implementations all had an interest in the protocols themselves being developed and being good.

So I really don't think the DE analogy is a good one. The thing that makes swapping DEs work is that a bunch of parties have broadly agreed upon all the major interfaces, and that consensus *is the hard part*. The standards don't exist for service managers, implementing them without that consensus is extremely risky, and designing / implementing them is extremely hard at a technical level in the first place.

A (completely hypothetical) experience journal of messing around with this stuff:

1. You choose something that isn’t systemd for pid 1. Ok cool.
2. How are you doing session management? elogind? Ok. So back to square 1, you need everything that systemd cares about cgroups and all laid out the way it expects, because you’ve put login1 on the bus, and a long tail of software is going to start calling it. If you don’t then what are you picking? I guess for a single user system maybe you don’t care, and you just do greetd + seatd.
3. You’d like to use network manager. Well network manager wants polkit. Guess what polkit is doing? using the logind dbus api to figure out if your requesting pid is in the session, because that’s part of the authorization verdict. Even worse: it uses systemd linked libraries to directly probe your session via the cgroups layout. So you can’t even mimic logind on the bus.
4. Fine you say, I don’t care about that, I’ll just sudo all of those commands, no active session required. News flash Network Manager isn’t managing any of your devices? Why? Because no-systemd means no udev. You *can* use mdevd if you are willing to shim with libudev-zero + carry patches (because it actually doesn’t work out of the box). Or you run eudev and admit that maybe, just maybe, the reason everyone is leaning on the systemd project is because they are the ones getting shit done. But also {uaccess} and {service} tagging in upstream rules isn’t going to work if you don’t have the service manager.

It’s not the init system, it’s the the plumbing for the whole thing. And I would argue that just swapping pid 1 for shit  and giggles and dragging in the rest of systemd in a trenchcoat is a pure aethestics waste of time, and likely to not work coherently anyway. And if you want to ship a super cut down desktop that’s fine, but that’s not what nixos is offering to people. People want functioning software, and sessions, auth, sudoless priv gain for guis, dynamic networking, all that needs to be available. Now I am definitely not stopping on my own personal quest to prove that a nice multi-seat nixos with zero-systemd is not just possible but desirable, but I would never have the gall to just suggest that *someone else* do it.

The argument that's been made repeatedly now is that the amount *less* that this can achieve is fundamentally limited by how much overlap there is between the commonly needed surface areas of service managers, and that this overlap is realistically very small. That means the benefit you describe for service manager portability is very small. An abstraction that only deals with the most trivial redundancies between implementations, with the rest constantly leaking through, is just noise, not useful. And that noise is a very real problem in terms of complexity and maintainability. For instance, as I've said before, when a package upstream provides their own systemd unit files, it's best for maintainability within NixOS to use those files; but that fundamentally eliminates the portability of it, since anything you'd be getting from a portable service definition would be in conflict with what you get from upstream. That's just one problem, but I think it speaks to the general category of problems about how high the friction is and how low the benefit is for modular services to be used as a portability mechanism.

To be clear, I like the aspects of modular services that have to do with being importable and that have to do with instancing (though, I do think even instancing has some pretty massive fundamental issues that warrant a lot more careful design work, and whose solutions would most likely make portability even more intractable). But portability just seems like a nonstarter to me because the benefit is very low unless the project becomes *very* big, and the cost is significant. It's for the best to just have disjoint interfaces for different service managers.

Making a portable interface for services whose purpose is to interact with their environment starts from making that interaction as tightly defined as possible. Something like flatpak but with a little more platform agnosticism and *even more tightly defined interfaces* to start out with in order to make that platform agnosticism achievable would make it very reasonable to use one interface for arbitrary platforms and organically grow it to support more and more over time. I am not saying this needs to happen tomorrow, but I think it might be a good direction to move towards.
